delegation-kanban.md: 'role=leaf loses all five' presented the blocklist as a uniform subtraction. Measured against a populated registry (88 tools), only delegate_task/clarify/memory/cronjob are removed by the two layers; send_message is never registered as an agent-callable tool at all (tools/send_message_tool.py:2264), so its blocklist entry is defensive only. Both layers remove toolsets BY NAME, never by member: the deny layer needs a non-empty tools list that is a subset of the blocklist (:1203-1204), the strip layer needs membership of _COMPOSITE_BLOCKED_TOOLSETS or an all-blocked list (:1180-1181), and kanban is dropped unconditionally (:1183) -- so a toolset pairing send_message with any unblocked tool matches neither predicate, and what keeps it out of the schema is the missing registration. Outcome unchanged (a leaf schema holds none of the five); mechanism corrected. The same probe also established that _strip_blocked_tools reads the STATIC TOOLSETS dict, so all(t in BLOCKED for t in []) is vacuously true and it drops 8 toolsets, not 5: safe, context_engine and hermes-gateway go as collateral even though hermes-gateway resolves to 72 tools at runtime.

audit_method: Static read of the working tree; no code executed. Verification battery, in order: (1) whole-repo identifier index sweep of every backticked symbol in all 14 module pages, then a targeted grep per flag; (2) AST walks (ast.parse) for every class/method/function span, public-surface count and enclosing-symbol question; (3) a symbol-adjacency sweep binding each file:NNNN citation to the identifier nearest before it and testing that identifier occurs within +/-3 lines of the cited line; (4) a fence-stack parse (opens==closes, empty stack) instead of a fence-count parity heuristic; (5) relative-link resolution for every markdown link; (6) index completeness against the module map. Instrument caveats, each learned by being fooled by it: the identifier index covered only .py/.ts/.tsx/.toml/.json and excluded tests/, docs/, evals/, website/, web_dist/, so C sources, SQL schema strings and test fixtures yielded false ABSENTs; `grep -l` piped to awk '{s+=$1}' sums a non-numeric field and can only ever report 0; a regex requiring trailing () matched none of a table listing bare names; split('|') on a two-column table puts the payload in cells[2], not cells[3]; and the last line of a fixed-width range dump is not an AST node's end_lineno. In every case the targeted probe, not the bulk instrument, was the arbiter. Of the 18 entries in audit_found_defects_fixed, 8 were introduced by my own hand-written or hand-edited prose rather than by the original workers, and were caught only because each edit was re-verified against source after it landed. an unpopulated tool registry makes every toolset resolve to [] , which is indistinguishable from genuinely-absent membership, so any claim about what a role can or cannot call was decided only after importing model_tools to trigger discovery (88 tools registered); a static read of the TOOLSETS dict alone under-reports, because resolve_toolset/validate_toolset merge registry-discovered tools at runtime. A second instrument caveat, learned the same way: the identifier index is a first-pass FILTER and never a completeness oracle. It held _stream_callback but not the bare stream_callback despite 76 real occurrences, so ABSENT from the index proves nothing and every flag was settled by targeted grep. A third: a message regex whose character class includes '-' must not be used to split Mermaid '-->>' arrows, because the greedy class eats a hyphen and the '->>' alternative then matches the remainder, manufacturing hyphenated pseudo-symbols out of correct participant IDs. A fourth instrument caveat, same origin: a node-count regex whose bracket group is optional matches every identifier on the line, so it tallies Mermaid message-label words as graph nodes and reported a spurious 67-node over-cap failure on a sequence diagram; the cap is also type-specific and does not bind sequence diagrams, which are measured in declared participants. Node counts must be taken by splitting on the arrow token and censusing declared participants, never by a permissive identifier sweep. A fifth instrument caveat, self-inflicted and worth pinning: compile() is the wrong oracle for documentation code fences. Signature sketches with '...' bodies, bare arrows and 'def' stubs are legitimate notation and compile() rejects them wholesale, so a fence-compile pass reported 7 of 8 fences invalid while every one of them was correct prose. Worse, the same pass had only detected 1 of the 8 fences in the first place, which is what made an earlier 'async def' claim look verified when it had never been parsed at all -- 'async def' is valid Python and the file was fine. A checker that silently under-counts is more dangerous than a checker that fails loudly. A sixth: a loop variable reused across a nested collection pass attributed all 5 identifier misses to the alphabetically last page; every attribution in a report must be re-derived from the bytes, not carried in a loop binding.
